# Squeezing gastruloids — unified parameter set

*Generated by `code/scripts/make_report.jl` from `results/phase_map.csv`
(20 runs, total compute 2.4 h).*

## 1. What this had to do

One set of mechanical parameters had to reproduce three separate observations:

1. **Fusion.** Two aggregates of pure cell type, placed in contact, must fuse the
   way the experiment says they do — and in particular the **B–C** pair must
   *glue* rather than round up into a single sphere.
2. **Polarisation** (unconfined). A spherical aggregate with an A,B core inside a
   C shell must polarise: A,B segregating to one pole.
3. **Patterns** (confined). Squeezed between plates of thickness `layers`, the
   A,B mass must break into **islands in a C sea**, above a critical initial
   cell number $N_0$ that grows with thickness.

## 2. The model

Cells are spheres of radius $r$ with a pairwise force, attractive between
contact and a cutoff $\mu r_{ij}$:

$$
F_{ij}(d) \;=\; f_{s_i s_j}\,\Bigl(\frac{r_{ij}}{d}-1\Bigr)\Bigl(\mu_{s_i s_j}\frac{r_{ij}}{d}-1\Bigr),
\qquad r_{ij}=2r,
$$

with $f=f_\mathrm{rep}$ for $d<r_{ij}$ and $f=f_\mathrm{att}$ above. Motion is
overdamped, with the drag shared over the $n_i$ contacting neighbours and a
neighbour-velocity alignment term $\alpha_\mathrm{ecm}$:

$$
\mathbf v_i \;=\; \frac{1}{\lambda n_i}\Bigl(\mathbf F_i + \alpha_\mathrm{ecm}\!\!\sum_{j\in\mathcal N(i)}\!\!\mathbf v_j\Bigr).
$$

Differentiation is one-way, $A\to B\to C$, with rates suppressed by the global
A fraction $f_A$:

$$
r_{AB}=\frac{p}{1+k f_A},\qquad r_{BC}=\frac{q}{1+k f_A}.
$$

$p$ and $q$ are **fixed** at the experimental values ($p\simeq 10q$) and were
never tuned here.

## 3. The parameter set

The final set is the collaborator's *fusion* set with **exactly two diagonal
entries of $f_\mathrm{rep}$ softened**:

```julia
mu    = 2 * [1    0.91 1    ;  f_att = 4 * [0.9 1.0 0.6 ;   f_rep = 3 * [3 1 1   ;
             0.91 1    1    ;               1.0 1.6 0.4 ;                1 1 1   ;
             1    1    1.07]                0.6 0.4 0.75]                1 1 1.7]
```

| | changed? |
|---|---|
| $\mu$ | no — collaborator's matrix |
| $f_\mathrm{att}$ | no — collaborator's matrix |
| $f_\mathrm{rep}$ off-diagonals, **[2,3] included** | no |
| $f_\mathrm{rep}[2,2]$ | $6\to3$ |
| $f_\mathrm{rep}[3,3]$ | $6\to5.1$ |
| $p,q$ | no |

**Why the softening is necessary.** With the stiff $f_\mathrm{rep}$ the A,B phase
never coarsens: at `layers = 1`, $N_0=500$ it stays a salt-and-pepper dispersion
(clustered fraction 0.31, largest cluster 12 cells) and simply differentiates
away. Softening the B–B and C–C self-repulsion lets it round up into compact
islands (clustered 0.86, islands of 23, 22, 21, 16, 14 cells).

**Why $f_\mathrm{att}$ is *not* rescaled.** An earlier version of this work used
$f_\mathrm{att}\times0.45$. That was tuned against a broken confinement (§4) and
is wrong: at $\times0.45$ the C–C and A–C pairs stop fusing altogether and the
monolayer islands dissolve. Note also that a uniform $f_\mathrm{att}$ scale is
**not** harmless — it preserves the *ratios* of surface and interfacial tensions,
hence contact angles, but $f_\mathrm{rep}$ is not scaled with it, so the
tension-to-elasticity ratio moves, and that is what decides whether an aggregate
can round up at all.

## 4. Two bugs that had been driving the conclusions

**(a) The plates did not confine.** The wall force was a *constant*,
`fz += rep_wall` while $z<r$. A constant force has no stable fixed point inside
the contact zone: it pushes the cell until $z\ge r$ and then switches off. At
`layers = 1` the band available to cell centres is only $L-2r = 0.1$, while one
restoring step displaces $\;\texttt{rep\_wall}\,\Delta t/(\lambda n_i)\approx0.075$,
so cells chattered straight across it.

| layers | cells outside the plates (old wall) | effective thickness |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **93 %** | 1.95 cells |
| 2 | 2 % | 2.02 |
| 3 | 0.3 % | 3.00 |
| 4 | 0.2 % | 4.00 |

Every earlier `layers = 1` result therefore described a buckled bilayer, not a
monolayer. The fix is a Hookean plate,

$$ F_z = \texttt{rep\_wall}\,\frac{r-z}{r}, $$

which vanishes at contact — so the contact point *is* the fixed point — and
cannot be outrun by in-plane crowding. Stability requires
$\texttt{rep\_wall}\cdot\Delta t<2$ (the $n_i<2$ branch of the equations of
motion drops the $1/n_i$ drag), giving `rep_wall = 60` at $\Delta t=0.015$ and
`150` at $\Delta t=0.0075$; larger values send the positions to `NaN`.

**(b) The readout was ~300 time units too late.** Since $A\to B\to C$ is one-way,
the A,B phase is a *transient* and $f_{AB}\to0$. Scoring each run at the first
frame with $f_{AB}\le0.12$ lands after the islands have both formed and begun to
erode. Runs are now scored over the whole trajectory (`island_timeline`), and a
run only counts as patterned if islands are present at the **end**; one that
fragments and then dissolves is reported as `transient`.

## 5. Results

### 5.1 Fusion

Two aggregates of 150 cells each, no division, no differentiation; the metric is
COM separation over $R_{g,1}+R_{g,2}$ ($\approx1.6$ at contact, $\approx0.5$ once
rounded into one sphere). Lower means more fused.

| pair | reference | this set | |
|---|---|---|---|
| AA | 1.614 | 1.702 | never fuses ✓ |
| BB | 0.537 | 0.531 | rounds up ✓ |
| CC | 0.562 | 0.536 | rounds up ✓ |
| **BC** | **0.947** | **0.744** | **glues, does not round** ✓ |
| AB | 0.470 | 0.138 | fuses |
| AC | 0.657 | 0.510 | fuses |

BC is the least-fused pair by a wide margin — every pair that does fuse sits at
$\le0.536$. This is predictable analytically: with
$W_{ij}=f_\mathrm{att}[i,j]\,2r\,A(\mu_{ij})$ where
$A(\mu)=(1+\mu)\ln\mu-2(\mu-1)$, the interfacial tensions
$\gamma_{ij}=\tfrac12(W_{ii}+W_{jj})-W_{ij}$ come out

$$ \gamma_{AB}=0.405,\quad \gamma_{AC}=0.232,\quad \gamma_{BC}=0.581, $$

so BC has the largest interfacial cost and every pair is in Steinberg's *partial
engulfment* class (a stable doublet with a finite contact angle).

**Caveat.** BC at 0.744 is more rounded than the reference 0.947. Softening
$f_\mathrm{rep}[2,2]$ and $[3,3]$ makes the B and C aggregates softer, so the
doublet rounds a little further before it stops. The ordering is right; the
number is not a match.

### 5.2 Polarisation (unconfined)


A 300-cell aggregate, A,B seeded as a spherical core inside a C shell, no
confinement. `offset` is the displacement of the A,B centroid from the aggregate
centre in units of the aggregate radius; $r_{AB}$ and $r_C$ are the mean radial
positions of the two populations.

| $t$ | $f_{AB}$ | offset | $r_{AB}$ | $r_C$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.503 | 0.018 | 0.576 | 0.880 |
| 160 | 0.377 | 0.225 | 0.427 | 0.790 |
| 320 | 0.209 | 0.594 | 0.656 | 0.672 |
| 480 | 0.109 | 0.789 | 0.827 | 0.615 |
| 640 | 0.053 | 0.920 | 0.946 | 0.620 |
| 700 | 0.044 | **0.945** | 0.973 | 0.637 |

The offset climbs monotonically and $r_{AB}>r_C$: the A,B cells segregate to one
pole and sit at the surface, C on the other side. It has not saturated by the end
of the run, so a longer $t_f$ gives a more completely separated end state.

![polarisation](code/figures/polarisation.png)

### 5.3b How well the plates actually confine

The Hookean wall settles at a penetration $\delta\simeq$ (in-plane crowding)/`rep_wall`
rather than at zero, so the slab is always a little thicker than nominal. The
nominal band for cell centres is $L-2r = 2.1\,(\text{layers})-2$.

| layers | $N_0$ | nominal band | measured z-spread | effective layers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100 | 0.10 | 0.11 | 1.01 |
| 1 | 200 | 0.10 | 0.23 | 1.06 |
| 1 | 300 | 0.10 | 0.13 | 1.01 |
| 1 | 500 | 0.10 | 0.13 | 1.02 |
| 1 | 750 | 0.10 | 0.16 | 1.03 |
| 2 | 340 | 2.20 | 2.71 | 2.24 |
| 2 | 500 | 2.20 | 3.37 | 2.56 |
| 2 | 750 | 2.20 | 3.69 | 2.71 |
| 2 | 1150 | 2.20 | 3.50 | 2.62 |
| 2 | 1700 | 2.20 | 3.45 | 2.60 |
| 2 | 2500 | 2.20 | 3.31 | 2.53 |
| 3 | 750 | 4.30 | 5.08 | 3.37 |
| 3 | 1150 | 4.30 | 5.39 | 3.52 |
| 3 | 1700 | 4.30 | 5.34 | 3.50 |
| 3 | 2100 | 4.30 | 5.30 | 3.48 |
| 3 | 2500 | 4.30 | 5.41 | 3.53 |
| 4 | 1700 | 6.40 | 7.21 | 4.39 |
| 4 | 2500 | 6.40 | 7.24 | 4.40 |
| 4 | 3200 | 6.40 | 7.36 | 4.46 |
| 4 | 4000 | 6.40 | 7.39 | 4.47 |

At `layers = 1` the sheet stays one cell thick (z-spread ≈ 0.11–0.23 against a
0.10 band) — this is the case the wall fix was for, and it works. At
`layers ≥ 2` the spring is *softer near contact* than the old constant force
was, so the slab runs thicker than nominal and the excess grows with $N_0$.
This is the flip side of the fix: a constant force drives the cell until
$z\ge r$ and switches off, which held the band tightly wherever the crowding
never exceeded it — that is, everywhere except the monolayer.

**Control.** `scripts/run_checks.jl wall` reruns `layers = 2`, $N_0 = 1700$ with
a 2.5× stiffer wall (`rep_wall` 150, $\Delta t$ 0.0075) and gets the *same
verdict*, so the classifications are not an artefact of the leak. The island
counts did differ (3 vs 4), consistent with the boundary sensitivity noted in
§6. If the thickness itself matters for a given question, use
`rep_wall = 150, dt = 0.005` at all thicknesses and pay the ~3× runtime.

### 5.4 Why the threshold grows with thickness

The obvious candidate is the **aspect ratio** of the A,B domain: it is a flat
disc of thickness $h$ (the slab) and in-plane diameter $D$, and like a liquid
sheet it might be expected to break up once it is wide enough relative to its
thickness. Taking the largest $D/h$ each run reached while its A,B domain was
still one piece:

| run | max $D/h$ | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| layers 4, $N_0$ 1700 | 5.46 | one blob |
| layers 3, $N_0$ 750 | 5.56 | one blob |
| layers 4, $N_0$ 2500 | 6.63 | one blob |
| layers 2, $N_0$ 340 | 6.66 | one blob |
| layers 3, $N_0$ 1150 | 6.85 | one blob |
| layers 4, $N_0$ 3200 | 7.49 | **islands** |
| layers 2, $N_0$ 500 | 8.05 | one blob |
| layers 3, $N_0$ 1700 | 8.34 | one blob |
| layers 4, $N_0$ 4000 | 8.38 | **islands** |
| layers 3, $N_0$ 2100 | 9.26 | **islands** |
| layers 2, $N_0$ 750 | 9.82 | one blob |
| layers 3, $N_0$ 2500 | 10.09 | **islands** |
| layers 1, $N_0$ 100 | 10.72 | one blob |
| layers 2, $N_0$ 1150 | 12.17 | **islands** |
| layers 2, $N_0$ 1700 | 14.75 | **islands** |
| layers 1, $N_0$ 200 | 15.16 | one blob |
| layers 2, $N_0$ 2500 | 17.88 | **islands** |
| layers 1, $N_0$ 300 | 18.56 | **islands** |
| layers 1, $N_0$ 500 | 23.95 | **islands** |
| layers 1, $N_0$ 750 | 29.35 | **islands** |

Blobs span $D/h$ = 5.46–15.16; islands span 7.49–29.35. **The ranges overlap**,
so no single cut on $D/h$ classifies these runs.


**The full scan does not support a universal $D/h$ threshold.** The two groups
overlap heavily: runs that stayed as one blob reached ratios well above ones
that broke up. Sorting by $D/h$ interleaves the outcomes rather than separating
them.

An earlier version of this write-up claimed $D/h\gtrsim5$ "separates every
run". That was based on seven exploratory runs and is **wrong** — with the full
20-point map the claim does not survive.

What the data does show is that the critical ratio depends systematically on
thickness, and in the *opposite* direction to the naive picture — thicker slabs
fragment at a **lower** aspect ratio:

| layers | highest $D/h$ still one blob | lowest $D/h$ that broke up |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 15.2 | 18.6 |
| 2 | 9.8 | 12.2 |
| 3 | 8.3 | 9.3 |
| 4 | 6.6 | 7.5 |


So a thin domain has to be proportionally much wider than a thick one before it
will break up. That is consistent with the monolayer being quasi-2D: rearranging
cells to pinch a domain in two requires neighbour exchanges that a single layer
cannot make out-of-plane, so break-up is kinetically suppressed there and the
domain simply stretches instead.

The geometric relation is still worth writing down. Since the domain packs
$n_{AB}$ cells into $h/2r$ layers,

$$
D \;=\; 4\sqrt{\frac{n_{AB}\,2r}{\pi h}}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
n_{AB} \;=\; \frac{\pi}{16}\Bigl(\frac{D}{h}\Bigr)^{2}\frac{h^{3}}{2r},
$$

so at *fixed* aspect ratio the cell count would grow like $h^{3}$. The measured
$N_0$ thresholds grow more slowly than that — see §5.3 — precisely because the
critical ratio falls with thickness, which partly cancels the $h^{3}$.

**Bottom line.** The model reproduces the experimental rule *thicker aggregates
need more cells to pattern* (§5.3), but the mechanism is not a single geometric
threshold. Geometry sets the scale; the kinetic competition between coarsening
and the one-way $A\to B\to C$ conversion sets where the line actually falls.

## 6. Caveats

* The adhesion scale is a **kinetic window**, not a free multiplier. At
  `layers = 1`, $N_0=500$: $\times0.70$ gives loose porous patches,
  $\times1.00$ compact stable islands, $\times1.40$ a single blob. The set sits
  at $\times1.00$ and is not far from either edge.
* BC fusion is qualitatively right but quantitatively more fused than the
  reference (§5.1). This is the one trade-off that could not be removed: the same
  softening that makes the islands work costs BC fidelity.
* `layers = 1` needs `rep_wall = 150` with $\Delta t=0.0075$; a wall stiff enough
  to hold the sheet flat is unstable at $\Delta t=0.015$. `wall_settings(layers)`
  selects this automatically.
* **One seed per phase-map point, and verdicts near a threshold are not robust.**
  This is not a generic disclaimer — it was observed directly. `layers = 1`,
  $N_0=200$ classified as `ISLANDS` at $\Delta t=0.0075$ and as `transient` at
  $\Delta t=0.005$, with everything else identical. The table brackets each
  threshold; it does not resolve it to better than roughly a factor of two, and
  the island *counts* at a boundary point should not be quoted as exact
  (the same run gave 3 islands at one timestep and 4 at another). Repeat over
  seeds before drawing a line on a figure.
* The islands are transient by construction: $f_{AB}\to0$, so run long enough and
  every pattern eventually dissolves into a pure C sea. The comparison window is
  $t\approx200\text{–}650$ (1 hour $=15$ model time units).

## 7. Reproducing this

```bash
# once
julia --project=code -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'

# the phase map (resumable; several hours)
julia -t auto --project=code code/scripts/run_phase_map.jl

# verification runs: polarisation, wall-setting equivalence, fusion assay
julia -t auto --project=code code/scripts/run_checks.jl all

# figures and this report
julia --project=code code/scripts/make_figures.jl
julia --project=code code/scripts/make_report.jl
```

`code/scripts/gastruloids_lib.jl` is **exported from the notebook** by
`code/scripts/export_lib.ps1`; edit the notebook, then re-export, so the two
cannot drift. `code/results/coms/*.jld2` are saved with `save_frames` (plain
arrays) rather than by pickling the `Community` — the latter does not reload,
because `ABM()` evaluates the generated step functions as anonymous closures in
`Main` and the pickle references them by gensym name.
